verses.text: Remember, Yahweh, what has come on us: Look, and see our reproach.
Our inheritance is turned to strangers, Our houses to aliens.
We are orphans and fatherless; Our mothers are as widows.
We have drunken our water for money; Our wood is sold to us.
Our pursuers are on our necks: We are weary, and have no rest.
We have given the hand to the Egyptians, To the Assyrians, to be satisfied with bread.
Our fathers sinned, and are no more; We have borne their iniquities.
Servants rule over us: There is no one to deliver us out of their hand.
We get our bread at the peril of our lives, Because of the sword of the wilderness.
Our skin is black like an oven, Because of the burning heat of famine.
They ravished the women in Zion, The virgins in the cities of Judah.
Princes were hanged up by their hand: The faces of elders were not honored.
The young men bare the mill; The children stumbled under the wood.
The elders have ceased from the gate, The young men from their music.
The joy of our heart is ceased; Our dance is turned into mourning.
The crown is fallen from our head: Woe to us! for we have sinned.
For this our heart is faint; For these things our eyes are dim;
For the mountain of Zion, which is desolate: The foxes walk on it.
You, Yahweh, remain forever; Your throne is from generation to generation.
Why do you forget us forever, And forsake us so long time?
Turn us to yourself, Yahweh, and we shall be turned. Renew our days as of old.
But you have utterly rejected us; You are very angry against us.

footnotes.content: The poet opens not with complaint, but with an appeal to memory: 'Remember.' This is prayer's first work—to place our sorrow before the Lord, not to hide it or pretend it away. Even reproach, acknowledged and witnessed, becomes bearable when brought to the foot of the only throne that lasts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dispossession cuts deep—the land your grandfather tilled, the home your mother kept, now in strangers' hands. When everything we built is taken, we learn whether we were clinging to the gift or to the Giver. That distinction matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Orphan and fatherless—the ancient words for vulnerability. And yet, God calls Himself the Father of the fatherless. That promise, spoken in Psalm 68, sits alongside THIS verse. The two truths don't erase each other; they hold each other in prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Water sold back to the thirsty, timber bartered by those who once owned the forests. When conquest strips away ownership, the conquered become tenants in their own necessity. Only mercy breaks that cycle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Weariness of this kind—pursued, never resting—grinds away the soul. But notice the prayer doesn't stop; it keeps speaking to the One who does rest, whose throne knows no fatigue. We lay our exhaustion before His inexhaustible mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To 'give the hand' is to make a covenant, to pledge allegiance. The defeated give their hands to whoever feeds them. Yet even when we believe we have no choice, we are learning—often bitterly—whom alone deserves our allegiance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children bear the weight of their fathers' sin—that is the shape of human history. Yet this verse itself becomes confessional; by speaking the truth, the people move toward acknowledgment and, finally, toward repentance. Truth spoken is the path toward healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Servants ruling over their masters: the world upside down, order inverted. When human rule fails this completely, we glimpse why the soul cries out for the only true Deliverer, the King whose kingdom flips every tyrant's throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bread earned at the peril of the sword. A meal is never simply a meal in conquered land—each bite is shadowed by risk. Yet the very fact that they still seek bread shows the human will to live persists even in devastation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Skin blackened, not from sin but from famine's heat. The body itself becomes a map of suffering. Yet the poet sees it, names it, and in naming it before God, refuses to let such anguish go unwitnessed. Prayer honors the suffering by speaking it aloud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The violation of women stands as the deepest shame of conquest—their bodies become spoils of war. These verses hold this horror unflinchingly. The Lord who weeps over this cruelty bends His ear to those who grieve it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Princes hanged, elders dishonored—the normal order is shattered. The gate (where elders sat in judgment) is no longer a seat of dignity. In exile, there is no honorable place to stand, and yet the prayer continues, addressing the Giver of honor beyond human sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Young men grinding at the mill—the labor of slaves and prisoners. Children stumbling under burdens never meant for their shoulders. The image is almost unbearable; yet the poem speaks it, and in doing so, refuses to forget, refuses to let cruelty pass in silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The gate where elders once counsel the city is silent; young men no longer sing. The gate was the heart of civic life. When grief is deep enough, even joy stops—the music ceases. Yet silence itself becomes prayer, and the One who made music still hears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joy and dance, turned into mourning. This is the ache of exile: not just hardship, but the loss of laughter itself. Yet the very fact that they knew joy once means they know what they've lost—and that memory, held before God, becomes part of their prayer for restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The crown fallen. But notice the turn: 'Woe to us! for we have sinned.' Here, beneath the lamentation, comes confession. The people are not saying others ruined them alone—they are acknowledging their own turning away. This humbling is the ground on which repentance stands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A faint heart, dimmed eyes—the physical language of despair and grief. Yet to speak it is to offer it. The prayer does not hide the pain but holds it up before the throne, knowing that the God who sees sees all of this.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zion desolate, foxes walking where the altar once stood—the holy mountain now a haunt of scavengers. The poet sees this devastation with his own eyes and names it before God. Such witnessing refuses to let the sacred place fall into forgetfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But You remain. This is the turn—the throne is not fallen like Zion's crown. Through all the ruins and despair, the God of eternity holds His throne from generation to generation. One verse of assurance in the midst of lament; enough to anchor prayer itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why do You forget us? The question echoes throughout scripture—the cry of the abandoned heart. Yet the very ability to ask 'why?' assumes Someone is listening. Complaint, when laid before God in prayer, becomes a form of faith: we believe He hears, even when we feel forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Turn us to yourself—the request is not for comfort alone, but for return to God. 'Renew our days as of old'—not a wish for the past, but a longing for restoration, for the kind of newness that only the Lord can grant. This is where lament ends: in the desire to be turned back to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The final word: utterly rejected, very angry. Readers today hear an echo in these last verses—not as prophecy, but as the cry of those who learned that judgment itself can be a form of mercy when it drives us back to God's feet. The anger of a God who cares enough to discipline is not the silence of an indifferent world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
